At 24 months, the instrumental need to develop this critical analytical capacity directly, rather than relying on AI-generated framing, remains firmly intact given no general-studies lock is even needed to make that case. Rating: Low.

By 2031, AI will generate more fluent-sounding feminist health critique, but the course's core competence — situating patriarchal medical history, intersecting oppressions, and reclaimed epistemologies within a defensible, source-grounded argument — still requires a human who can judge whether that framing is accurate rather than merely plausible-sounding pastiche dressed up in the right vocabulary. The verification burden stays high because errors in this domain, such as misattributed oppression narratives or flattened intersectional nuance, are non-obvious to an unprepared reader, precisely the failure mode task-exposure research associates with contested normative content resisting easy substitution by a model. No institutional mandate protects the course, but the dampening effect of persistently high oversight need does the protective work instead across this horizon. Rating: Low.

A decade out, AI will be markedly more capable at producing plausible critical-health-feminist prose, and the honest uncertainty is how much that erodes the course's role in training students to evaluate such prose critically. The central case still holds that it does not fully erode: evaluating and constructing rigorous intersectional health critique, distinguishing genuine feminist historiography from confident-sounding but ungrounded synthesis, remains a verification-heavy task resistant to unsupervised AI substitution, per the jagged-frontier finding that miscalibrated trust persists even as raw model capability continues to rise steadily. Absent a general-studies or licensure lock, the protection here is entirely the high oversight burden inherent to normatively contested subject matter of this kind. Rating: Low, with real uncertainty about how far this holds by 2036.
SOC 3920.d: This course focuses on health issues specific to women and the challenges historically faced by women in the health care arena. Students will learn about the role of patriarchal medical mythologies that exist throughout various cultures in the oppression of women, especially minority women, and how women have reclaimed healing, health, and communities of medical knowledge production. This course specifically explores feminist, physiological, psychological, and sociological factors in women's health within a global context.

r: Students examine evolving social trends in work — demographics, technology, and industry growth — and link personal biography to career choice across a variety of industries, occupations, and professions, a content-synthesis and trend-interpretation task. Observed-usage data already shows Computer & Mathematical and office/writing tasks as the largest categories of current AI use, and this course's core work — researching labor-market trends and drafting career-trajectory analyses — falls squarely in that band. Productivity research also finds AI assistance disproportionately uplifts less-experienced users on exactly this kind of research-and-writing task, which is instructive for undergraduates still developing this skill. Still, with no general-studies designation and no deployment yet inside how this specific course is taught, the instrumental need to build this analytical capacity in class remains largely intact at 24 months. Rating: Medium.

By 2031, AI tools will fluently research and synthesize labor-market and technology trends and connect them to individualized career narratives, the exact task this course assigns students each term, and task-exposure research already classifies this kind of writing- and analysis-heavy work as strongly exposed to AI substitution over time and across occupations broadly. No institutional lock or foundational-scaffolding role protects the course from that erosion, so the instrumental case for taking it specifically to build this trend-analysis skill weakens substantially over this horizon. The rating rises to High: automation-vs-augmentation data suggests such advisory and analytical writing tasks are increasingly automated outright rather than merely assisted, consistent with the shift observed between consumer and enterprise API usage patterns generally. Rating: High.

A decade out, career-trend research and biography-to-occupation matching is a well-trodden AI-competent task, and the central case has this fully absorbed into commodity career-guidance tools available well outside any college classroom setting entirely, freely, and on demand for anyone. Without a general-studies mandate or scaffolding role, there is little structural reason the course's specific instrumental function — teaching students to research and reason systematically about work trends — survives in anything resembling its current form through 2036. The genuine hedge is that macro-level diffusion research shows firm-level AI adoption still lagging raw capability considerably, so how quickly career-services pedagogy itself restructures around ubiquitous tools is less certain than the underlying task capability curve alone truly is. Rating: High, moderately hedged.
SOC 4160.d: Students in this course examine the evolving social trends surrounding work in contemporary society (e.g. demographics, technology, industry growth, etc). Student biographies' are linked to their career choices as they examine factors associated with gaining employment in a variety of industries, occupations, and professions.

r: The course examines relationships within and among stratification systems, how scarce resources are distributed across them, and the resulting effects on social identity and social mobility — an evidence-synthesis and analytical-writing task drawing on established sociological data and theory. Task-exposure research finds this class of analytical, non-adversarial synthesis strongly positively associated with AI exposure, and observed-usage data confirms such writing already constitutes a large and growing share of current deployment in both consumer and enterprise contexts. At 24 months, however, the course carries no general-studies designation, and classroom delivery of stratification analysis has not yet been displaced by deployed AI tooling in sociology instruction; competent capability has not translated into adopted pedagogical substitution this soon. The instrumental need to take the course stays largely intact for now. Rating: Medium.

By 2031, AI will fluently generate comparative analyses of stratification systems, mobility patterns, and resource-distribution effects, the same synthesis work this upper-division course assigns each term to its students, and with no general-studies lock or foundational-scaffolding role to slow that erosion the instrumental case strengthens meaningfully toward High for this elective. Automation-vs-augmentation data suggests such document-style analytical tasks increasingly shift from assisted to substituted, particularly in professional and academic writing contexts already well documented in observed-usage studies of current deployment. Some hedge remains because stratification analysis often engages contested empirical claims about inequality where jagged-frontier miscalibration could sustain some in-class verification training, but the base erosion of the content-delivery function is the larger effect operating at this horizon. Rating: High.

A decade out, the central case is that AI-generated stratification analysis is materially indistinguishable in competence from a well-trained student's own independent work, consistent with fast capability growth in analytical-writing tasks generally across disciplines and fields of study broadly and consistently over time. No institutional mandate or scaffolding role protects this course from that trajectory through 2036. The genuine uncertainty concerns how sociology programs restructure such courses — toward critiquing and verifying AI-generated stratification claims rather than producing comparable analysis entirely from scratch on their own — rather than whether the underlying synthesis capability itself arrives; that pedagogical restructuring is considerably harder to forecast than the raw capability curve itself proves to be. Rating: High, hedged on implementation timing rather than direction.
SOC 4200.d: Examine the relationships within and among stratification systems, the distribution of scarce resources, and the consequent effects on social identity and social mobility.

r: Students analyze patterns of gender and sexual violence through queer/trans theory and transnational feminism, examining how safety and precarity are unevenly distributed across groups and covering sexual, interpersonal, family, and trafficking violence alongside state, carceral, medical, and military violence in multiple contexts. This is contested, normatively dense, positionality-sensitive material where jagged-frontier research findings — that AI users are measurably less accurate and poorly calibrated outside a model's reliable zone — are directly on point: confidently generated analysis of gender-based violence can sound authoritative while flattening the theoretical nuance the course is specifically built to teach its students. That elevated verification burden, not any institutional mandate, keeps the instrumental need to build this analytical capacity directly, under instructor guidance, intact at 24 months. Rating: Low.

By 2031, AI will produce more fluent prose engaging queer/trans theory and transnational feminist frameworks around violence, but the course's real competence — judging whether that framing correctly represents how precarity and safety are unevenly distributed across specific populations — remains a verification-heavy task few students could check unaided without close guidance. Task-exposure research separately notes that critical-thinking-intensive work is negatively associated with exposure even as writing tasks are positively associated, and this course sits closer to the former: the analytical judgment, not the surface prose generation, is the graded competence being built here across each unit. No general-studies designation protects the course, but the high oversight burden inherent to contested, high-stakes social-justice content does that protective work instead. Rating: Low.

A decade out, AI capability for generating plausible-sounding gender-and-violence analysis will be substantially higher, and the honest uncertainty is whether verification burden erodes as models improve at representing marginalized experience accurately and contextually across diverse populations and settings worldwide over time. The central case still holds it does not fully erode: the jagged-frontier finding that miscalibrated trust persists even as capability rises applies with particular force to intersectional analysis of violence, where getting the framing subtly wrong carries real interpretive and ethical costs for the populations discussed in the course. Absent an institutional lock, the course's instrumental necessity rests entirely on this persistent verification demand, semester after semester. Rating: Low, with acknowledged uncertainty about how far AI narrows this gap by 2036.
SOC 4240.d: Students analyze key patterns and structures of gender and sexual violence, with a special focus on the diverse experiences of women, queers and gender-variant people. Students draw from disciplines such as queer/trans theory and transnational feminism to illuminate iterations of and resistance to gender-based violence, including how 'safety' and 'precarity' are distributed unevenly across groups due to various social formations. Topics in this course include sexual violence, interpersonal violence, family violence, trafficking, state violence (including carceral, medical and military violence), among others.

r: This variable-topics seminar involves intensive study and critical analysis of major sociological theorists — Weber, Durkheim, Marx, Simmel, Mannheim, Mills, and Parsons — or selected theoretical systems in classical and contemporary sociology, a task centered on close textual interpretation and contested exegesis rather than factual synthesis. Task-exposure research finds critical-thinking-intensive work strongly negatively associated with AI exposure, distinct from the writing-heavy tasks that are positively associated, and theoretical exegesis sits squarely in the negatively-associated category: getting a theorist's argument subtly wrong is a non-obvious failure a novice reader cannot easily catch on their own. At 24 months this verification burden, not any institutional mandate, keeps the instrumental need to work through primary theory under expert seminar guidance fully intact. Rating: Low.

By 2031, AI will produce fluent-sounding summaries and comparisons of Weber, Durkheim, Marx, and other canonical theorists, but distinguishing a genuinely rigorous reading from a plausible misreading remains a task requiring someone who already knows the material well and can spot subtle distortion in the argument — the jagged-frontier finding that users are poorly calibrated about AI reliability outside its competence zone applies directly to contested theoretical interpretation of this kind. No general-studies designation protects this advanced seminar, but the elevated verification burden inherent to theory exegesis performs that protective function instead across this horizon. The course's role preparing majors for graduate-level theoretical literacy further tempers erosion, though its variable-topics structure means specific content shifts with each offering. Rating: Low.

A decade out, AI models will handle theory summarization and comparison with much greater fluency, and the genuine uncertainty is whether that erodes the course's rationale for close, instructor-guided textual engagement with primary theorists themselves rather than summaries alone, over extended discussion. The central case holds that it does not fully erode: critical theoretical interpretation remains the kind of contested, high-stakes-for-accuracy work the task-exposure literature associates with resistance to substitution, and the seminar's role in building majors' capacity to evaluate, rather than merely consume, theoretical claims persists through this horizon and well beyond it too, in the central case. Rating stays Low, though this is among the more contestable ratings in the batch given how fast general reasoning capability has been advancing recently.
SOC 4350.d: Content varies, but each course involves intensive study and critical analysis of major sociological theories, such as those of Weber, Durkheim, Marx, Simmel, Mannheim, C. Wright Mills, and Parsons; or of selected theoretical systems in contemporary or classical sociology.

r: This continuation of the department's research-methods sequence applies advanced quantitative techniques — designing studies, computer coding, and computer-assisted statistical analysis of individual and group research projects — entirely digital, well-specified tasks with checkable outputs. Controlled studies of AI coding assistance already show large realized speedups on exactly this kind of statistical and data-analysis coding work, and observed-usage data confirms Computer & Mathematical tasks are the largest current category of AI use, meaning both competence and actual deployment are already present at 24 months, unlike more nascent applications elsewhere in the sociology curriculum. The course carries no general-studies designation, and its fully digital, code-centric nature, combined with only moderate verification burden, removes the usual protective factors that hold other courses down. Rating: High.

By 2031, GDPval-style evaluations of real analytical deliverables show models approaching parity with human experts on comparable tasks, and quantitative survey-research work — statistical coding, data cleaning, model specification, and results drafting — is precisely the kind of well-documented, digital, iteratively-checkable task that trend favors most strongly of all. The verification burden is real but manageable: statistical output is checkable against established methodological standards rather than requiring adversarial or ethically fraught judgment, which keeps the course from qualifying for the dampening protection other courses in this batch receive. No accreditation or general-studies lock exists to slow the shift either. The instrumental case for taking this specific course to acquire hands-on quantitative-coding competence continues eroding toward AI-assisted or AI-performed execution. Rating: High.

A decade out, capability-trend research describing rapid growth in AI's usable task horizon points toward routine, competent execution of the entire quantitative-research pipeline this course teaches — study design, coding, and computer-assisted analysis — becoming the default rather than the exception in practice across the discipline and well beyond it too. With no institutional mandate and a fully digital task profile, there is little structural brake on this trajectory continuing through 2036. The main uncertainty is not whether the coding and analysis tasks become AI-competent, which appears likely in the central case, but how quickly quantitative-methods pedagogy itself pivots toward directing and auditing AI-run analyses rather than hand-executing every step. Rating: High, with high confidence in the direction of travel.
SOC 4600.d: This course is a continuation of SOC 3600 - Research in the Social Sciences. It focuses on the application of advanced quantitative research techniques, including individual and task-group assignments intended to develop students' skills in designing, organizing, computer coding, and doing computer-assisted analysis of selected research projects.

r: This is a supervised, in-service field placement conducted with participating agencies and institutions across the urban social-service landscape — direct, embodied, real-time engagement with clients, coworkers, and institutional settings, with specific requirements set by the placement agency rather than by a syllabus alone. Task-exposure research consistently places hands-on, in-person, interpersonal service work in its low-exposure categories, distinct from the desk-based analytical and writing tasks AI already handles well in other parts of the curriculum. Diffusion data shows only a modest share of US firms and agencies have adopted AI tools even for back-office functions, let alone for embodied field supervision, so realized deployment inside social-service field placements is essentially absent at 24 months. The instrumental need for direct, supervised field experience is fully intact. Rating: Low.

By 2031, AI will likely assist with case documentation, intake paperwork, and administrative components surrounding field placements, but the core requirement — a student physically present at a partner agency, building professional judgment through supervised real-time interaction with clients and staff — remains an embodied, interpersonal task entirely outside what AI performs directly for the student in the field. Task-exposure research's low-exposure classification for manual and physically co-present service work continues to apply at this horizon, and adoption-lag evidence suggests agency-level AI diffusion into direct practice settings remains gradual even as general model capability keeps rising elsewhere. No general-studies designation is needed to sustain the rating; the embodied nature of supervised fieldwork does the protective work entirely on its own. Rating: Low.

A decade out, the administrative tasks surrounding field placement — scheduling, note-taking, resource lookup — will likely be substantially AI-assisted, but the placement's defining requirement remains a student's embodied presence in agency settings, building situational judgment and professional rapport that cannot be supplied remotely by any model or chatbot, however capable it eventually becomes at that point. Institutional brakes on this move slowly: even where diffusion of administrative AI tools accelerates inside social-service agencies generally, direct client-facing supervised practice is the kind of physically co-present, real-time work the task-exposure literature treats as durably resistant to substitution over time. The hedge concerns how much of the surrounding administrative burden shifts, not whether embodied field practice itself remains required for every student. Rating: Low.

r: This capstone continues the department's methods sequence into qualitative techniques — ethnography, participant-observation, unobtrusive research, unstructured interviews, and content analysis — carried out through a hands-on research project tied to each student's own interests. Interviewing and participant-observation are real-time, interpersonal, presence-dependent tasks that task-exposure research places among lower-exposure categories, distinct from purely textual synthesis work; and interpretive validity in qualitative analysis depends on reflexive judgment that is hard for a novice to verify in AI-generated output, an elevated verification burden the jagged-frontier literature associates with miscalibrated trust in unfamiliar domains. At 24 months, with no general-studies designation but strong embodiment and verification protections in place, the instrumental need to build these fieldwork and interpretive skills directly remains intact. Rating: Low.

By 2031, AI will assist meaningfully with transcript coding and content-analysis pattern-finding, the portions of this course's toolkit that are more textual and digital in nature and thus more tractable to automate reliably at scale across large datasets. But the defining competences — conducting an unstructured interview that builds genuine rapport, sustaining participant-observation in the field over time, and judging whether an interpretive claim is grounded rather than merely convenient — remain interpersonal and reflexively verification-heavy in ways the jagged-frontier and low-exposure interpersonal-task findings both support. As this course is explicitly the department's qualitative capstone, no later required course depends on it, but that terminal status does not by itself erode the instrumental need for the underlying fieldwork skill. Rating: Low.

A decade out, AI tools will likely handle transcription, initial coding, and pattern surfacing across large qualitative datasets quite capably, meaningfully changing the workload profile of qualitative research generally and how it gets taught in graduate and undergraduate seminars alike across many programs nationally. Yet the central case still requires a human conducting the interview, present in the field, and exercising the reflexive judgment needed to validate interpretive claims against lived context — precisely the interpersonal, presence-dependent, high-verification-burden work that has proven durably resistant across the evidence base cited throughout this batch. The genuine uncertainty is how much the analytic back-half of qualitative work shifts to AI assistance, not whether the human fieldwork core itself remains necessary for the degree. Rating: Low.
SOC 4710.d: This capstone course is a continuation of SOC 3600 - Research in the Social Sciences. It focuses on the application of advanced qualitative research techniques, such as ethnography, participant-observation, unobtrusive research, unstructured interviews, and content analysis. Students gain hands-on experience in various qualitative methods and analysis techniques while carrying out a research project related to their area of interest.
